description: Generative models, Large Language Models, prompt engineering, RAG, dense embeddings, hallucination mitigation, and responsible AI alignment.

topics.name: Generative AI Fundamentals
topics.definition: Generative AI refers to deep learning models capable of synthesizing novel, realistic content (text, images, audio, code, video, and 3D assets) that mimics patterns learned from training data.
topics.explanation: Generative models model the joint probability distribution P(X, Y) or data distribution P(X), allowing them to sample and generate entirely new synthetic instances. In contrast, Discriminative models learn conditional probability P(Y|X) to classify or separate data points. Major generative paradigms include: (1) Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs: generator vs discriminator zero-sum game); (2) Variational Autoencoders (VAEs: latent probabilistic encoding and reconstruction); (3) Diffusion Models (iterative noise addition and learned reverse denoising, powers Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, DALL-E); (4) Autoregressive Transformers (next-token text/code generation).
topics.example: A diffusion model generating a photorealistic digital painting of an astronaut riding a horse on Mars given a natural language prompt.
algorithm_steps: Curate massive multi-modal training dataset (billions of images or tokens)
Train model to predict missing noise, next tokens, or latent probability distributions
At inference: sample from latent random distribution z or seed with prompt prompt_0
Iteratively decode or denoise latent vectors into final high-resolution output media
advantages: Generates novel, high-fidelity synthetic creative assets, text, and computer code on demand
Accelerates human ideation, drafting, software development, and graphic design
limitations: Prone to fabricating incorrect claims (hallucinations) with persuasive fluency
Severe training carbon footprint and copyright infringement concerns
applications: Automated software engineering copilots (GitHub Copilot, Cursor)
Personalized educational tutoring and creative writing assistance
suggested_followups: Difference between Generative and Discriminative models?

topics.name: Large Language Models (LLMs)
topics.definition: Large Language Models are massive deep neural network language models containing tens to hundreds of billions of parameters, pre-trained on vast internet-scale text corpora to understand and generate natural language.
topics.explanation: Modern LLMs are predominantly decoder-only autoregressive transformers. Training follows a three-stage pipeline: (1) Self-Supervised Pretraining: model learns next-token prediction P(w_t | w_{<t}) on trillions of tokens, internalizing grammar, world knowledge, and reasoning patterns; (2) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): training on curated instruction-response pairs to learn helpful dialog behavior; (3) Alignment (RLHF / DPO): Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback or Direct Preference Optimization to ensure outputs are helpful, harmless, and honest. LLMs exhibit 'emergent abilities' such as in-context few-shot learning and chain-of-thought reasoning as model scale exceeds critical thresholds.
topics.example: Models like GPT-4, Claude 3.5, Gemini 1.5, and LLaMA 3 generating software applications, solving Olympiad math problems, and answering complex scientific questions.
algorithm_steps: Pre-training: optimize billions of parameters on trillions of tokens via causal language modeling loss
Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT): train on curated high-quality conversational demonstrations
Reward Modeling: train a scoring model on human preference rankings of model responses
PPO / DPO Optimization: align policy to maximize reward while penalizing drift from base model
Inference: sample next tokens using temperature, top-p (nucleus), and repetition penalties
advantages: Remarkable conversational fluency, reasoning versatility, and cross-domain zero-shot generalization
Understands diverse computer programming languages and natural human tongues
limitations: Hallucinations: states false or fabricated claims with unwavering confidence
Knowledge cutoff: static weights cannot know events occurring after training completion without tools like RAG
Massive compute cost and lack of strict formal guarantees
applications: Conversational AI assistants, code generation, summarization, document analysis, automated agents
suggested_followups: What are the three stages of training an LLM?
What is RLHF (Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback)?
How do rule-based chatbots compare to LLMs?

topics.name: Prompt Engineering
topics.definition: Prompt engineering is the empirical discipline of structuring, optimizing, and crafting input text prompts to guide generative AI models toward producing accurate, consistent, and desired responses.
topics.explanation: Because LLMs are conditioned on prior context, prompt phrasing significantly alters output quality. Key techniques include: (1) Zero-Shot Prompting: giving direct instructions without examples; (2) Few-Shot / In-Context Learning: providing 2-5 input-output demonstration pairs in the prompt; (3) Chain-of-Thought (CoT): instructing the model to 'think step by step', breaking multi-stage reasoning down; (4) Role Prompting / System Prompts: specifying persona, constraints, and target audience; (5) Directional / Structured Output Prompts: specifying JSON schemas or Markdown formats and using XML/triple backtick delimiters to prevent prompt injection.
topics.example: Using Few-Shot Chain-of-Thought prompting to solve a math word problem by demonstrating: 'Q: Roger has 5 tennis balls... A: Let\'s think step by step: He buys 2 cans of 3 balls (2*3=6). 5 + 6 = 11. Answer is 11.'
algorithm_steps: Define clear objective, role persona, and expected output format (e.g. JSON schema)
Provide explicit context, constraints, and negative constraints (what NOT to do)
Include high-quality few-shot examples demonstrating edge cases
Append chain-of-thought reasoning triggers ('think step-by-step before answering')
Iteratively test and refine prompts across diverse test inputs to measure output consistency
advantages: Requires zero model retraining or weight updates (operates entirely at inference time)
Immediate iteration and fast deployment of customized agent behaviors
limitations: Heuristic and fragile: minor prompt rewording or model version updates can break output formatting
Consumes input context window tokens, increasing API latency and billing cost
applications: System instructions for AI agents, customer support formatting, automated code generation
suggested_followups: Difference between Zero-Shot and Few-Shot prompting?

topics.name: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
topics.definition: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is an AI architecture that enhances language models by retrieving relevant authoritative documents from an external knowledge base and feeding them into the model prompt as grounding context.
topics.explanation: RAG bridges the gap between static LLM parametric memory and dynamic external facts. The RAG pipeline consists of: (1) Indexing: documents are chunked into 200-500 word passages and converted into dense embedding vectors stored in a Vector Database (Pinecone, Milvus, Chroma, Qdrant); (2) Retrieval: when a user asks a question, the query is embedded, and cosine similarity retrieves the top-k most semantically relevant chunks; (3) Generation: the retrieved chunks are injected into the prompt along with the user query, instructing the LLM to generate an answer grounded exclusively in the retrieved facts.
topics.example: An enterprise internal HR chatbot: An employee asks 'What is our 2026 paternity leave policy?'; the system retrieves Section 4.2 of the company handbook and generates an accurate, cited answer without hallucinating.
topics.formula: P(y \mid x) = \sum_{z \in \text{Top-}k} P(z \mid x) \cdot P(y \mid x, z)
algorithm_steps: Ingest, clean, and chunk enterprise documents into semantic passages
Generate dense vector embeddings for all chunks and index in a Vector DB
When user queries: convert user query to embedding vector
Perform approximate nearest neighbor (ANN) vector search using Cosine Similarity
Rerank top retrieved chunks using a cross-encoder model
Assemble prompt: System instructions + Retrieved passages + User query
Pass grounded prompt to LLM to synthesize cited response
advantages: Drastically mitigates hallucinations by grounding answers in verified source documents
Updates model knowledge in real-time simply by updating the database, avoiding costly model retraining
Provides direct source citations and traceable provenance for answers
limitations: Retrieval failures: if the retriever fails to find the right chunk, the generator produces poor answers
Chunking strategies and context length limits can truncate essential cross-document context
applications: Enterprise document search, legal research assistants, medical reference tools
suggested_followups: What are the steps of a RAG pipeline?

topics.name: Dense Embeddings and Vector Search
topics.definition: Dense embeddings are fixed-length, low-dimensional continuous vector representations generated by neural models that capture high-level semantic meaning, enabling mathematical similarity comparisons across text, code, or images.
topics.explanation: Unlike sparse lexical encodings (TF-IDF, Bag-of-Words) where words must match exactly, dense embeddings map semantically similar sentences to proximal coordinates in vector space (e.g. 768 or 1536 dimensions). For instance, 'How do I reset my password?' and 'Forgot login credentials' have zero word overlap, but high cosine similarity in embedding space. Vector databases use Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) index algorithms like Hierarchical Navigable Small World (HNSW) graphs to search millions of vectors in single-digit milliseconds.
topics.example: Generating 1536-dimensional embeddings for 1,000,000 legal contracts and finding all clauses semantically equivalent to 'indemnification upon breach of contract' in 4 milliseconds.
algorithm_steps: Pass text string through transformer encoder (e.g. text-embedding-3-small or BGE)
Extract mean-pooled token representations to form single vector representation
L2-normalize vector to unit length
Index vector in HNSW graph structure within a vector database
Query database using cosine inner-product to return top-k nearest neighbors
advantages: Captures semantic intent, synonyms, and conceptual relationships beyond literal keyword matches
Universal representation supporting multi-modal cross-media retrieval (text-to-image)
limitations: Can struggle with exact keyword lookups (e.g. part numbers, exact product SKUs) where sparse BM25 search excels
Compression loss: squeezing a long 500-word paragraph into a single vector inevitably loses fine details
applications: Semantic search engines, RAG knowledge retrieval, recommendation engines, facial verification
suggested_followups: What is HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World)?
Why combine BM25 and Dense Embeddings (Hybrid Search)?
How is Cosine Similarity calculated for embeddings?

topics.name: Hallucinations and Factual Reliability
topics.definition: Hallucination in AI refers to the phenomenon where a generative model produces plausible-sounding, syntactically fluent statements that are factually false, unfaithful to source context, or completely fabricated.
topics.explanation: Because autoregressive language models predict the next most probable statistical token rather than querying an internal truth database, they can confabulate convincing non-existent facts, fake legal citations, or false medical advice. Types include: (1) Intrinsic Hallucination: output directly contradicts given source context; (2) Extrinsic Hallucination: output asserts unverifiable claims not supported by any source. Mitigation strategies include: Grounded RAG, Chain-of-Verification (CoVe), Self-Consistency decoding, constrained decoding, and hybrid rule-based fact verification.
topics.example: A lawyer submitting a legal brief written by ChatGPT containing six fabricated court decisions with fictitious judge names and citations that the model made up out of thin air.
algorithm_steps: Inject authoritative grounding documents into context via RAG
Instruct model with strict negative constraints ('Answer only using provided text; if unsure, state I do not know')
Use low temperature decoding (0.0 to 0.2) to minimize stochastic drift
Apply automated factuality checking pipelines (e.g. TruLens, Ragas, ROUGE)
Cross-reference outputs against deterministic rule-based knowledge bases
advantages: Awareness of hallucinations is essential for deploying safe, production-grade AI systems
Combines well with rule-based systems to provide deterministic factual guardrails
limitations: Cannot be 100% eliminated in purely statistical foundation models due to the probabilistic nature of next-token prediction
applications: AI governance, legal tech compliance, clinical healthcare AI verification
suggested_followups: How does Rule-Based AI eliminate hallucinations?

topics.name: Responsible AI and Safety Alignment
topics.definition: Responsible AI is the practice of designing, developing, and deploying artificial intelligence systems that are ethically grounded, fair, transparent, accountable, robust against malicious misuse, and aligned with human values.
topics.explanation: Key pillars of Responsible AI: (1) Fairness: preventing demographic and socioeconomic bias; (2) Transparency & Explainability: enabling human understanding of automated decisions; (3) Privacy & Security: protecting personal data against extraction and model inversion; (4) Safety & Alignment: ensuring models refuse harmful requests (e.g. cyberweapons, CBRN synthesis, self-harm) via Constitutional AI and reinforcement learning from AI feedback (RLAIF); (5) Robustness: defending against jailbreaking and adversarial prompt attacks; (6) Accountability: establishing human-in-the-loop audit trails and watermarking synthetic media.
topics.example: An LLM guardrail system (like Llama Guard or NeMo Guardrails) intercepting and blocking a user prompt attempting to jailbreak the system into generating malware instructions.
algorithm_steps: Establish formal ethical principles and safety policy taxonomies
Red-team model to discover vulnerabilities, toxicity, and jailbreak vectors
Apply Constitutional AI: critique and revise outputs according to written ethical principles
Deploy input/output guardrails to filter sensitive keywords and toxic intents in real time
Continuously audit deployed models against emerging regulatory standards (EU AI Act)
advantages: Prevents severe societal harm, reputational damage, and legal liability
Builds sustainable user trust and adheres to international regulatory frameworks
limitations: Over-alignment / sycophancy: overly conservative guardrails can lead to false refusals of benign educational queries
applications: Enterprise conversational AI guardrails, content moderation, automated red-teaming
